questions.prompt: What is the worst-case lower bound for any comparison-based sorting algorithm?
questions.explanation: A decision tree sorting n elements has n! leaves, so its height — the worst-case comparison count — is at least log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n).

questions.prompt: What is counting sort's time complexity for n integers with keys in [0, k]?
questions.explanation: Counting sort tallies keys and places elements in O(n + k); it is efficient when k = O(n) and is stable.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Radix sort uses a stable sort on each digit
Non-comparison sorts beat Ω(n log n) by not comparing elements to each other
Counting sort works directly on arbitrary floating-point keys over any range

questions.explanation: Counting sort is stable, radix relies on per-digit stability, and these sorts index by key value rather than comparing. They need bounded integer keys, so (d) is false.

questions.prompt: The worst-case lower bound for any comparison sort is Ω(n log ___). (fill the missing term)
questions.explanation: log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n), so comparison sorts require Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of counting sort.

items.text: Tally the number of occurrences of each key
Convert the counts to prefix sums (output positions)
Place each element into the output using its position

questions.explanation: Count occurrences, turn them into cumulative positions, then place each element directly — no comparisons involved.

questions.prompt: Match each sort with its key fact.

pairs.right: O(n + k), integer keys in a small range
Stable pass per digit, O(d·(n + k))

questions.explanation: Each linear-time sort exploits key structure; comparison sorts are bounded below by Ω(n log n).
